turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: You want to examine how students travel. What would make your survey different from the one conducted last year?

turns.speaker: Nina
turns.text: Last year students were simply asked if they owned a bicycle. I’d like to know how people actually came to campus on a particular day.

turns.speaker: Jon
turns.text: We thought about asking them to remember every trip over the last month, but people might leave out short journeys.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. Ask about the most recent weekday, and include the outward and return journeys separately. Those journeys may involve different modes.

turns.speaker: Nina
turns.text: We were going to stand outside the car park to recruit people.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: That would be fast, but you would meet more drivers than people who walk or take the bus. Try inviting randomly selected students by email. Send one reminder to anyone who hasn’t replied, then record the response rate.

turns.speaker: Jon
turns.text: Do you think we should collect addresses so we can calculate distance?

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Collect the first part of the postcode only if you need broad location information. For your question, asking about journey time will be simpler. No exact addresses.

turns.speaker: Nina
turns.text: We’ll ask how long each leg took. Should we also ask why people chose that mode?

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Yes. Offer a short list such as cost, convenience and lack of alternatives, and include a space for an answer you hadn’t considered.

turns.speaker: Jon
turns.text: We have to deliver a report in three weeks. Can we start collecting responses next Monday?

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Test the form with five students first. Ask them to explain each question aloud. If their interpretations match what you intended, you can distribute it on Wednesday.
